## 1. 5. Service management > 5.3 Service design and development
Source: Government Functional Standard GovS 005: Digital (`govs-005`), Government Digital Service. Authority: mandatory. page last updated 2026-10-01.
Cite inline as: ([Government Functional Standard GovS 005: Digital: 5.3 Service design and development](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital-html#service-design-and-development))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [MANDATORY] "Services shall be delivered in accordance with the Service Standard."
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "Service Manual", pages about 1.2 years apart: "COTS products and services must be designed to meet the specific needs of the users of your service." https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/commercial-off-the-shelf-products-and-services#user-centred-design
- [MANDATORY] "Services shall be monitored using consistent service performance measures (see 5.6), reviewed quarterly."
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "Service Manual", pages about 1.2 years apart: "COTS products and services must be designed to meet the specific needs of the users of your service." https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/commercial-off-the-shelf-products-and-services#user-centred-design

- [RECOMMENDED] "New, changed or transformed services should provide value to government and users, and be usable and efficient."
- [RECOMMENDED] "User research (see 8.3), iterative development and, where appropriate, testing of AI-enabled components should continue throughout the service life cycle."
- [RECOMMENDED] "Where services are not digital, or perform poorly against usability and efficiency measures, the service owner should consider redesigning the service end-to-end."
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "Service Manual", pages about 9.7 years apart: "The service owner should decide if what you’ve recorded is an acceptable risk for your service." https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/test-your-services-performance#assess-the-risk
  - Possible conflict (machine-suggested, NOT verified): similar wording in "Service Manual", pages about 7.4 years apart: "When you’re confident you want to move on to beta, your delivery manager and service owner should start working on a beta business proposal." https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-alpha-phase-works#deciding-whether-to-move-on-to-beta
- [RECOMMENDED] "Organisations buying off-the-shelf products, services or AI-enabled tools should ensure suppliers can meet user needs and relevant standards."
- [RECOMMENDED] "Note: Where AI is used in a service, it should be used only where there is clear evidence of user need, with appropriate human oversight, assurance, transparency, security and monitoring."

Section text (verbatim):
> New, changed or transformed services should provide value to government and users, and be usable and efficient. See GovS 002, Project delivery.
> Services shall be delivered in accordance with the Service Standard. [footnote 2]
> User research (see 8.3), iterative development and, where appropriate, testing of AI-enabled components should continue throughout the service life cycle.
> Services shall be monitored using consistent service performance measures (see 5.6), reviewed quarterly.
> Where services are not digital, or perform poorly against usability and efficiency measures, the service owner should consider redesigning the service end-to-end.
> Organisations buying off-the-shelf products, services or AI-enabled tools should ensure suppliers can meet user needs and relevant standards. See 6.3 and GovS 008, Commercial.
> Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with by embedding cyber security into digital services, including any AI-enabled components, throughout the life cycle.
> Note: Advice and guidance about technology choices can be found in the Technology Code of Practice. [footnote 3]
> Note: Where AI is used in a service, it should be used only where there is clear evidence of user need, with appropriate human oversight, assurance, transparency, security and monitoring.
> Note: The Service Manual includes advice on creating and running public services that meet the Service Standard. [footnote 11]

## 2. Service design and policy design
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-10-22, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Service design and policy design](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/understanding-and-meeting-policy-intent#service-design-and-policy-design))

Section text (verbatim):
> Service teams are expected to deliver new, existing or changing policy when they are developing a service. Both policymakers and service teams face similar challenges in translating government priorities into policies and services that affect people’s lives.
> Policy teams design, develop and propose solutions to help meet ministerial objectives based on research and evidence. They ensure the effective delivery of policy, evaluating its impact and adapting as necessary.
> Many government departments are trying to embed user-centred design into policy making. Service teams may have the opportunity to work with policy professionals to design a range of policy options so that ministers can make more informed decisions about which one to follow. Your role may involve highlighting unintended consequences and risks and showing how a particular policy might not work.
> You can find out more about policy making by:
> completing an Introduction to policy on Civil Service Learning
> reading a short guide to policy for government digital professionals
> reading a Policy Lab blog post on Introducing a ‘Government as a System’ toolkit
> joining the policy design community

## 3. Chapter 5: Equality, diversity and inclusion > 5.6 What to consider in managing equality, diversity and inclusion > 5.6.2 Design for inclusion
Source: The Teal Book: Project delivery in government (`teal-book`), Government Project Delivery. Authority: advisory. text last seen to change 2026-10-15 (re-read weekly from the publisher's daily PDF).
Cite inline as: ([The Teal Book: Project delivery in government: 5.6.2 Design for inclusion](https://projectdelivery.gov.uk/teal-book/home/part-a-project-delivery-in-government/chapter-5-equality-diversity-and-inclusion/#:~:text=5.6.2%20Design%20for%20inclusion,-Decisions%20on%20solution))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "Solution design and development should ensure that equality, diversity and inclusion considerations are understood by the design and development teams before work begins, and that the relevant expertise is available, so that these are factored into the work as it progresses."

Section text (verbatim):
> Decisions on solution design and development are critical in determining how well the solution works for different users and influences the outcomes delivered and social value generated by the work. Solution design and development should ensure that equality, diversity and inclusion considerations are understood by the design and development teams before work begins, and that the relevant expertise is available, so that these are factored into the work as it progresses.
> User-centred design practices, in particular, play an important role in ensuring that a solution meets the current and future needs of users in an accessible and inclusive way, and meets statutory requirements on accessibility. These include obligations under the Equality Act 2010 which require all public services to be accessible to everyone who needs them, including services only used by public employees; and specific provisions on access to digital services under the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations (2018), which cover websites and mobile applications and apply to all public sector bodies. Further information on this is set out in the Government Functional Standard for Digital and in associated guidance on GOV.UK.
> Designing for inclusion and accessibility is not just about meeting the needs of specific identified groups, however. All users can have different needs at different times and in different circumstances: their ability to use a service could be temporarily affected by their location, health or equipment, for example. Beware, too, of making assumptions about user needs. Bringing in first-hand user experiences, developing and validating user stories and journeys – virtually or, even better, physically – helps bring breadth of thinking into the team.
> Consider also how the solution is to be validated, assured and implemented. For example:
> are delivery partners aware of inclusion requirements?
> have the needs of different groups been included in trials?
> are guidance and signage accessible to all?
> does a service rollout prioritise larger user groups and leave minority groups, for example those requiring special adjustments, to the end?
> is a solution required to meet all identified user needs as a condition of acceptance, or is there a risk that some minority user needs might be passed to operations to sort out as part of ‘snagging’? Such issues can have a significant impact on whether or not a solution is felt to be inclusive by users, and on subsequent take up, as well as on wider reputation.
> More information on user needs and requirements, solution design and delivery is set out in Part F: Solution delivery.
> See Achieving inclusive outcomes by design (requires sign in) for further support on embedding equality, diversity and inclusion in solution design within the project life cycle.

## 4. 5./6. Conduct the evaluation and align the analysis > When delivering a service in‑house
Source: The Sourcing Playbook (`sourcing-playbook`), Government Commercial Agency. Authority: mandatory (comply or explain). page last updated 2026-09-30.
Cite inline as: ([The Sourcing Playbook: When delivering a service in‑house](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-sourcing-and-consultancy-playbooks/the-sourcing-playbook-html#when-delivering-a-service-inhouse))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "Delivering a service using internal resources and expertise should be based on the same robust expectations set out in the Playbook for outsourced services."
- [RECOMMENDED] "To help achieve these standards, you should consult the following sections in the Playbook:"
- [RECOMMENDED] "Quality data and asset registers (see Preparing to go to market): We should be collecting and maintaining data about our assets and services to enable us to make informed decisions when we need to."
- [RECOMMENDED] "Where similar services are insourced and outsourced by a contracting authority, comparable KPIs should be set to enable fair and consistent comparison of delivery models and service levels."

Section text (verbatim):
> Delivering a service using internal resources and expertise should be based on the same robust expectations set out in the Playbook for outsourced services.
> This includes setting and monitoring performance against clear objectives and outcomes managed by appropriately qualified individuals. This is set out in detail in the government’s project delivery standards.
> To help achieve these standards, you should consult the following sections in the Playbook:
> Piloting the delivery of a service (see Chapter 4: Piloting delivery of a Service): Testing a service on a small scale before full‑scale implementation can provide organisations with valuable data on a service and / or test best practice approaches.
> Quality data and asset registers (see Preparing to go to market): We should be collecting and maintaining data about our assets and services to enable us to make informed decisions when we need to.
> KPIs and baselines (see Chapter 5: Preparing to go to market): Ongoing monitoring linked to intended benefits in a proportionate and appropriate way is essential for all public services.
> Where similar services are insourced and outsourced by a contracting authority, comparable KPIs should be set to enable fair and consistent comparison of delivery models and service levels.
> The Infrastructure and Projects Authority offers expertise in all aspects of project delivery including training, guidance and resources.

## 5. Using participatory methods for design
Source: Test, Learn and Grow Playbook (`test-learn-grow-playbook`), Cabinet Office. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2026-10-19.
Cite inline as: ([Test, Learn and Grow Playbook: Using participatory methods for design](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/test-learn-and-grow-playbook/designing-test-ideas-phase-3#using-participatory-methods-for-design))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "When designing your prototype, you should involve:"

Section text (verbatim):
> In this phase, you’ll use participatory design to create a testable prototype alongside the people who will use or deliver the service.
> When designing your prototype, you should involve:
> people with lived experience of the issue
> operational staff who work in government or voluntary, community or social enterprises (VCSEs)
> Staff in VCSEs may work in services connected to the challenge area, or know people with lived experience. Include them when you:
> decide what to prototype
> design the prototype
> Work with them as equal decision makers from the start, or create opportunities for feedback by running design workshops or show and tells.
> Always make sure you conduct research safely and compensate members of the public for their time.

## 6. Types of fraud > Consider the weaknesses of online services
Source: Service Manual (`service-manual`), Government Digital Service. Authority: advisory. page last updated 2024-10-22, over a year ago.
Cite inline as: ([Service Manual: Consider the weaknesses of online services](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/protecting-your-service-against-fraud#consider-the-weaknesses-of-online-services))

Obligations in this section (verbatim, strength from the modal verb):
- [RECOMMENDED] "If you’re moving an offline service online, you should consider any new weaknesses that may be introduced in the process."

Section text (verbatim):
> If you’re moving an offline service online, you should consider any new weaknesses that may be introduced in the process.
> Online services are more open to fraud and fraudsters can try multiple attempts in a short space of time.
> Do not assume any security processes you’re following offline will fully protect your service from fraud when the service moves online.
> Learn about discovering vulnerabilities during service design, development and deployment to address security weaknesses and prevent fraud.
